authors.name: Ingrid Albuquerque-Solomon
authors.bio: A writer in Bangalore who runs Single Mom Meets, a monthly support group for single mothers. She publishes her contact number in the newspapers.

authors.name: Jenny Svetec
authors.bio: Writes on the Hebrew scriptures and what they ask of the people who read them.

articles.title: When Serpent Suicide Slithers in
articles.deck: It was 10.45 at night when a stranger rang Ingrid Albuquerque-Solomon to say she was going to die. She had walked that road herself, which is the only reason the call kept going.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the July 2013 issue. Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is the author's throughout. Pull quotes have been drawn from her own text. The author died on 2 May 2023; republication rights now sit with her estate and have not yet been confirmed.

body.v: A young and desirable Indian actress, just 26, committed suicide by hanging herself from the ceiling. The reality of individuals retreating into despair has shaken not just Bollywood. On the heels of that tragedy, there have been several other suicides. Can anything change the tide?
It was 10.45 in the night when a person called to tell me she was committing suicide. She had already called her friends to say goodbye.

She did not know me; she'd only called because she promised her best friend she would. The details of my Single Mom Meets appear in the newspapers with my contact number, which her friend had jotted down.

Her story: She was eight-and-a-half months pregnant, had not yet reached her first anniversary and her husband had left her for another woman. Over the next hour, I was given heart-wrenching details of the humiliation she'd had to endure.
Life has nothing to offer us and I have no choice but to opt out, I hope you understand.

I had walked that road myself. She wanted to know how I was still alive. I informed her that I too had tried to make one last call before blowing out the candle. I'd rung up a spiritual companion to say goodbye. I told her about other single moms who'd also struggled at the same cliff-hanging edge, but survived. We met once a month to encourage one another; now we are not without joy, hope and a promising future for ourselves and our children in our uplifted lifestyles.
She cancelled her death plans and asked to join the group.
Everybody — especially in today's mercurial and mercenary times — needs to have a spiritual companion.

Everybody – especially in today's mercurial and mercenary times – needs to have a spiritual companion (distinct from a friend or family member) with whom he or she can set up a weekly God-present confidential meeting where they can be mutually accountable to one another, encourage and advise one another.
So that God can use them as instruments to speak to and through one another, it is best if they are not friends (who could be emotional rather than objective and righteous in counsel).
That way, when all doors appear firmly closed and serpent suicide comes slithering in, the God-friend can open the window and let the sun come shining in.

Lord, You are the Way, the Truth and the Life! Please be there for those who are drowning in darkness and have lost the will to live. At that desperate moment, rescue them and give them light and fresh new hope for the future.

Ingrid Albuquerque-Solomon died on 2 May 2023. She kept writing about this subject for the rest of her life, including a later piece called "Thinking About Suicide? Let's Talk". This page is republished with that in view.

This piece is about suicide. If any of it is close to where you are now, please talk to someone you trust, or contact a helpline in your country. In India, Tele-MANAS is free and runs around the clock on 14416.

articles.title: This is the Camp that God Built
articles.deck: Jenny Svetec on Numbers 5, a Hebrew word that means to move in permanently rather than rent, and what was actually waiting for the people who got sent outside.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the July 2013 issue. Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is otherwise the author's. Pull quotes have been drawn from the text; nothing has been reworded.

body.v: Remember the childhood story, “This is the House that Jack Built”? Well the book of Numbers could be titled, “This is the Camp that God Built.”

In the first chapters of Numbers, God ordered a census for Israel, establishing each tribes' position in the camp, as He assigned rooms for all His children. Each tribe was then relayed their numbers, what order they were to march out of camp and where they were to camp in relation to the tabernacle. Sounds almost like family camp, when cabins are assigned and the information booklets are handed out, doesn't it?

After instructing Moses about the details of the tabernacle, and seeing His people respond with obedience and generosity in the establishing of the “tent that God built”, suddenly God takes an unexpected turn in construction details. God commands Moses to move everyone with leprosy, those with oozing sores, those menstruating, and those whom had been at a deathbed out the camp. Moses and the Israelites quickly obeyed.
Hold on: Cast out the grieving, the ill, women menstruating and men with discharge? What was going on here?

In order to unlock the principle, a crucial key is to hear what God is saying: Put out both male and female, put them outside the camp, that they may not defile their camps in the midst of which I dwell (Numbers 5:2, NKJV).
Dwell, shakan, in Hebrew, is a word which means to permanently move in and settle down.
body.highlight: permanently move in and settle down

body.v: You see, it was almost moving day in Camp Israel. God's intention was to permanently settle as the centre of Israel, with all His power and His presence, the Hub of His people, with the twelve tribes settled like spokes around the tabernacle, a massive bird's eye illustration of God as the focal point of life for His people.

In order for God to move in, certain ground rules had to be maintained. Camp Israel, by virtue of God's Presence, had to maintain a standard which pagan, Egyptian-raised Israel would not be expecting: the camp needed to be holy. Upon uttering His intention for permanent residency, Moses acted quickly, for God was not suggesting a conditional rental agreement, a twelve month lease, easily broken and quickly abandoned. God was outlining His desire to stay with His people and Moses eagerly moved to meet His conditions.
Holiness to God is by its nature, uncompromising.

For the people of Israel, whose living experience of worship was limited to Egyptian idol worship and wilderness groans, leaving the tabernacle to the priests seemed normal. Yet God, in establishing His residency, informed Israel that His greatness impacted more than His tabernacle; in fact, by virtue of His holiness, anywhere God lived had to be holy, set apart, which meant the entire nation would be impacted, without exception. Hence the decree that all with leprosy, discharge or exposed to a corpse needed to leave.

Quite the object lesson. Notice the set standard. Basically, Moses said: If you are unclean, get out. This is no ordinary KOA campground. This is Camp Israel. God is our midst. We are not an ordinary nation. We are extraordinary.

For anyone ill, Camp Israel was not exactly a comfortable environment, though it was definitely an honest one. Yet why was discharge such an offense? And what was the problem with leprosy? Why banishment for being near a corpse?

In Israel's days, leprosy, a contagious disease of the flesh, was a literal illustration of the decay process, one slow day at a time, until disease overtook the afflicted one. Discharge was a sure outward sign that illness was present in an individual and unchecked illness always lead to death. Corpses were deadly, literally with the threat of disease multiplying the longer the body decayed.

With the command to remove those near death and diseased, God, the Giver of Light, firmly illustrated that He will not live with our darkness. Darkness and light can't cohabitate. One encompasses the other. Just as light can't cohabitate with darkness, so death cannot abide with the Source of all life.

With the command for the diseased to leave camp, the Israelites understood what holiness actually meant – no wiggle room, no excuses, no rationalizing of sin, death or disease. If you were diseased, you were out. No exceptions. God was in the camp and His Presence would have a huge impact on Israel. God's terms of His occupation with Israel were clear: Be holy, as I am holy. Be whole, be set apart and be honest with the condition of your sin. With God present, Camp Israel could never be a place where anything goes. The defiled and ill, the contagious had to leave, because the Holy One was coming to stay.

But what of those put out? What of the women, who were thrust outside of the settlement trying to understand the God who had removed them from the camp? What of the lepers who were banned from the camp? Or those dazed with grief at the death of their mother, father, or child?
Outside of the camp is where His mercy and healing flows deepest.
body.highlight: where His mercy and healing flows deepest

body.v: The book of Leviticus brings us an answer with good news for the diseased and grieved in Israel: Outside of the camp is where His mercy and healing flows deepest. For beyond the camp was God's infirmary, where the diseased were healed, the grieving were restored and the priesthood was at its best.

For the leper, Leviticus 14:3,7 explains how the priesthood was more than equipped to deal with this disease, stating: And the priest shall go out of the camp, and the priest shall examine him; and indeed, if the leprosy is healed in the leper… And he shall sprinkle it seven times on him who is to be cleansed from the leprosy, and shall pronounce him clean, and shall let the living bird loose in the open field.

Leprosy wasn't a death sentence with God around. In fact, the outskirts of the Israelite camp was actually a place of healing, not banishment. When the priest journeyed out of the camp to verify the miracle, and the man or woman was declared clean once again, he let loose a bird to fly so that all the camp could see that restoration had happened.

For a woman with discharge, Leviticus 15 offered similar days, cleansings and offerings. For the man with discharge, Leviticus 15 established clear expectation for the man to wait, to clean, to atone and to be restored.

God's intention for the camp outskirts was for healing, not neglect. Outside of the camp, the individual would wait for healing, and then a merciful and compassionate priest would bring relief, declare the person healed and welcome them back into the camp where God lives. Unlike Egypt, God, Jehovah Ropha, the God of Healing lived at Camp Israel, thus restoration and mercy ruled the day. If an Israelite journeyed outside the camp to find God in their darkness, they could return to God in the camp and be transformed by His light.

Now consider, if God required holiness for the people of Israel, a stern reckoning of sin, which was transparently addressed and ministered to, what does God require for us, His people, who are temples for Him, the living God? Peter, in his letter says not much has changed on that account:

Therefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and rest your hope fully upon the grace that is to be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ; as obedient children, not conforming yourselves to the former lusts, as in your ignorance; but as He who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, because it is written, “Be holy, for I am holy.” (1 Peter 1:13-16, NKJV)

God hasn't changed his plans. He still plans to permanently dwell within us. As we rend our hearts before Him, we need to remember the place of mercy outside of the camp, that beloved cross of Calvary for our diseased hearts, fleshy minds and broken bodies. Let's go to our great High Priest who loves and gave Himself for us and receive the forgiveness and healing needed, that we may return to live a life which glorifies God.
May we each humble our hearts and allow the Holy Spirit to lead us in holy living as we delight in the Camp which God built, to His great glory and to our great wonder.
